title: The Library That Never Sleeps (with an information panel)
subject: English
source: Written for english/y6 lesson 57 (Teacher's unseen text: The Library That Never Sleeps (an original story about a future library, with an information panel; written for this lesson))

passage.title: The Library That Never Sleeps
paras: The new library opened on the first day of spring, on the top floor of the tallest building in our town. My mum said it was the future. I said it was just a library with a lift.

I was wrong. The moment the doors slid apart, the shelves began to move. They glided across the polished floor like skaters, rearranging themselves so that the books you might want were always the ones nearest to you. Above them, small lights floated, glowing softer when someone sat down to read.
Then there was the librarian. It was a robot, tall and thin, with a round screen for a face that showed a single, patient line. 'Good morning,' it said. 'What are you curious about today?'
On that first day, I kept my distance. I did not trust anything that could find a book faster than I could think of one. I sat in the furthest corner and pretended to read a cookbook.
But the library never closes. It is open at dawn, when the city is grey and quiet, and it is open at midnight, when the stars press against the glass roof. So I went back. And back again.

By the second week, the robot knew my name. By the third, it knew that I liked stories about the sea and hated stories where the dog dies. It never told me what to read. It only asked questions, and waited, and somehow its questions always led me somewhere new.

One evening, I found it standing alone by the window, its screen dimmed, as if it were watching the rain. 'Do you ever read?' I asked. 'Every book,' it said, 'but never for the first time.' I did not know what to say to that.

Now, when I arrive, I take two chairs from the reading circle. I sit on one, and I save it a seat on the other. It never sits down. But it always comes over, and we talk about the book I am reading, and the library hums quietly around us, awake, as it always is.

panels.title: Libraries of the future (information panel)
points: Some libraries already use robots to sort returned books and to carry them to the right shelf.
Many libraries are open longer hours, with self-service machines for borrowing at night.
Experts say that people will still need librarians: to help them find reliable information and to choose what to read next.
A library is not only a building for books. It is a free place to learn, to think and to be with other people.

questions.q: R: Where is the new library?
questions.a: On the top floor of the tallest building in the town.

questions.q: R: When did it open?
questions.a: On the first day of spring.

questions.q: I: What did the narrator first think of the library? Give a quotation.
questions.a: She was unimpressed: 'just a library with a lift'.

questions.q: V: The shelves 'glided'. What does this suggest?
questions.a: They moved smoothly and quietly.

questions.q: V: What is compared to 'skaters'?
questions.a: The shelves.

questions.q: R: What happens to the floating lights when someone sits down to read?
questions.a: They glow softer.

questions.q: R: What shows on the robot's screen?
questions.a: A single, patient line.

questions.q: I: How did the narrator feel about the robot at first? Give evidence.
questions.a: Wary: she 'kept her distance' and sat in the furthest corner.

questions.q: I: Why did she pretend to read a cookbook?
questions.a: To look busy and avoid the robot.

questions.q: R: What time does the library close?
questions.a: It never closes.

questions.q: R: What kind of stories does the narrator like?
questions.a: Stories about the sea.

questions.q: E: Why does the narrator keep going back?
questions.a: It is always open, and the robot's questions lead her to new books.

questions.q: V: Find a phrase that shows the stars were very close to the roof.
questions.a: 'press against the glass roof'

questions.q: I: What does the robot mean by 'never for the first time'?
questions.a: It already knows every book, so it can never enjoy discovering one.

questions.q: I: How does the narrator feel about the robot by the end? Give evidence.
questions.a: Fond of it: she 'saves it a seat'.

questions.q: E: Why might the writer end with the library 'awake, as it always is'?
questions.a: It links back to the title and the idea that it never closes, giving a calm, circular ending.

questions.q: R: From the information panel, name one way libraries already use robots.
questions.a: Sorting returned books and carrying them to the right shelf.

questions.q: R: From the panel, why will people still need librarians?
questions.a: To find reliable information and choose what to read next.

questions.q: S: Summarise the story in two sentences.
questions.a: A girl distrusts a robot librarian in a library that never closes. Over time she grows fond of it and saves it a seat.

questions.q: P: Is the story fiction or non-fiction? How do you know?
questions.a: Fiction: invented characters and events; the panel is the non-fiction part.
